intro: Everything has a name. Your mom, your dog, your chair and your book all have names. In this unit you learn Spanish names for the people, pets and things around you.
In Spanish, a little word comes before each name. It is el or la, and both mean the. You will learn the -o and -a clue that helps you pick. Then you can say Esta es mi mamá and Es un libro.
bigQuestion: How do el and la help us name the people and things around us?

timeline.t: Say la mamá, el papá and el bebé
Name pets: el perro, el gato, el pez, el pájaro
Learn that el and la both mean the
Use un, una and mi: Esta es mi mamá
Name things at school and at home
Use the -o and -a clue to pick el or la
Ask ¿Qué es? and answer Es un... or Es una...

words.d: the mom — say ma-MÁ
the dad — say pa-PÁ
the sister; el hermano is the brother
the dog — roll the rr
the cat — a pet that says meow
the book — you read it
the table — ends in -a, so la
my — mi mamá, my mom

test.why: Hermana ends in -a and goes with la.
A cat says meow. El gato is the cat.
Mi means my. La abuela is the grandma.
Silla goes with la and una: una silla.
Mano ends in -o but uses la: la mano.

test.q: ¿Qué es? It is a dog. You say...
test.why: Perro goes with el and un: Es un perro.

test.q: What do el and la mean?
test.why: El and la both mean the. Un and una mean a.
Día breaks the -a clue. We say el día.

write.prompt: Draw your family or your room. Label three people or things with el or la, like la mamá or el libro. Then say one sentence: Esta es mi... (This is my...).
tips: Check el or la for each word. Look at the last letter.
Remember the rule-breakers: el día and la mano.
Say your labels out loud to a friend.

title: El and La: Naming Things

chapters.title: My Family and My Pets
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we name the people and animals we love in Spanish?

story.title: Name Tag Day
story.kicker: Everyone at the family photo gets a name tag, even the cat.
paragraphs: It is photo day for the Soto family. Lucía has a box of name tags. She wants to put one on everybody. She holds up the first tag. It says la mamá (the mom).
Lucía puts la mamá on her mom. She puts el papá (the dad) on her dad. Her big brother gets el hermano (the brother). Grandma smiles at her tag. It says la abuela (the grandma).
Then the baby crawls in. Lucía laughs. "Es el bebé (It is the baby)!" The dog barks. The cat hides under a chair. Lucía makes two more tags: el perro (the dog) and el gato (the cat).
Click! Everyone is in the photo. Lucía points and says, "Esta es mi mamá (This is my mom)." Every tag has a little word in front. Some say el. Some say la. Lucía wonders why.
story.think: Why do you think some tags say el and some say la?

lessons.title: Mom, Dad and the Baby
lessons.mainIdea: La mamá is mom, el papá is dad, and el bebé is the baby.
reading: Look at a family photo. Point to the mom. Say *la mamá* (the mom). Point to the dad. Say *el papá* (the dad).
Now point to the baby. Say *el bebé* (the baby). Listen to the end of mamá, papá and bebé. The last part is loud. The mark on top tells you.

words.d: the mom — the mark on the last a makes it loud: ma-MÁ
the dad — say pa-PÁ, loud at the end
the baby — say be-BÉ

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at the photo. A mom holds a baby. The baby has a red hat. A dad stands next to them. He is tall. He is smiling.
look.prompt: Point to each person and say la mamá, el papá or el bebé.

check.why: La mamá means the mom.
El papá means the dad.
El bebé means the baby.

lessons.title: Brothers, Sisters, Grandparents
lessons.mainIdea: A boy is el hermano, a girl is la hermana.
reading: A boy in your family is *el hermano* (the brother). A girl is *la hermana* (the sister). The words look alike. Only the end is different: -o for the boy, -a for the girl.
Grandpa is el abuelo (the grandpa). Grandma is *la abuela* (the grandma). See it again? -o for the boy word, -a for the girl word.

words.d: the brother — ends in -o
the sister — ends in -a
the grandma; el abuelo is the grandpa

look.title: Two Words, One Letter Apart
look.text: el hermano → la hermana. el abuelo → la abuela. Change the -o to -a. Change el to la. Now the word is for a girl or a woman.
look.prompt: Say the word for grandpa. Now change one letter to say grandma.

check.why: La hermana is the sister. El hermano is the brother.
El abuelo is the grandpa. It ends in -o.

check.q: Which word is for a girl?
check.why: La hermana ends in -a and means the sister.

lessons.title: The Dog and the Cat
lessons.mainIdea: El perro is the dog, and el gato is the cat.
reading: Woof! That is *el perro* (the dog). Roll the rr in perro. Your tongue buzzes: pe-rrrro.
Meow! That is *el gato* (the cat). Both words start with el. Both end with -o. Many -o words go with el.

words.d: the dog — roll the rr
the cat — a pet that says meow

look.title: Who Is Hiding?
look.text: A brown dog sits by the door. His tail wags. A gray cat sleeps on the bed. She is curled up in a ball.
look.prompt: Point to each pet and say its name in Spanish.

check.why: El perro means the dog.
A cat says meow. El gato is the cat.

check.q: Which little word goes with perro?
check.why: We say el perro. Perro ends in -o and goes with el.

lessons.title: The Fish and the Bird
lessons.mainIdea: El pez is the fish, and el pájaro is the bird.
reading: A fish swims in a bowl. It is *el pez* (the fish). Pez is a short word. Say it fast: pes.
A bird sings on a branch. It is *el pájaro* (the bird). Say PÁ-ja-ro. The mark on the first a makes it loud.

words.d: the fish — a pet fish in a bowl
the bird — say PÁ-ja-ro

look.title: Pets in Our Class
look.cite: Example class count, made up for practice
look.prompt: Which pet do the most kids have? Say its name in Spanish.

check.why: El pájaro means the bird.

check.q: It swims in a bowl. It is...
check.why: A fish swims. El pez is the fish.

check.q: Which part of pájaro is loud?
check.why: The mark on the á makes PÁ the loud part.

lessons.title: El and La Mean The
lessons.mainIdea: El and la both mean the. Each name has its own one.
reading: In English we say the. In Spanish there are two words for the: *el* and *la*. We say el papá. We say la mamá.
Each word has its own partner. El perro. La hermana. Learn the little word with the name, like a pair of shoes.

words.d: the — goes with words like papá, perro, gato
the — goes with words like mamá, hermana, abuela

look.title: Find the Partner
look.text: Here are the name tags: ___ mamá. ___ papá. ___ gato. ___ abuela. Each one needs el or la in front.
look.prompt: Say each tag with el or la in front.

check.why: Mamá goes with la: la mamá.
Gato goes with el: el gato.

check.q: What do el and la mean?
check.why: El and la both mean the.

lessons.title: Un, Una and Mi
lessons.mainIdea: Un and una mean a. Mi means my.
reading: El goes with *un* (a). Say un perro (a dog). La goes with *una* (a). Say una abuela (a grandma).
Now make it yours. *Mi* means my. Mi gato is my cat. Say it with a smile: "Esta es mi mamá (This is my mom)."

words.d: a — un perro, a dog (for el words)
a — una hermana, a sister (for la words)
my — mi papá, my dad

look.title: Show Your Family
look.text: Maya holds up a photo. She says, "Esta es mi mamá." Then she points to a dog. She says, "Es mi perro." (It is my dog.)
look.prompt: Draw your family. Point and say Esta es mi... for each person.

check.why: Mi means my. Mi gato is my cat.
Hermana goes with la, so it uses una: una hermana.
Perro goes with el, so it uses un: un perro.

review.why: Abuela goes with la. We say el papá and la mamá.
Esta es means this is. Mi means my. Mamá is mom.
A dog says woof. El perro is the dog.
Abuela goes with la and una: una abuela.

chapters.title: Things in My Room and School
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a word's last letter help us guess el or la?

story.title: The Classroom Treasure Hunt
story.kicker: Señor Díaz hides a clue on every thing in the room.
paragraphs: Señor Díaz has a game today. He hid clues all over the classroom. "¡Vamos! (Let's go!)" he says. Tomás and Rosa run to find the first clue.
The first clue is on el libro (the book). It says, "Look under la mesa (the table)." Rosa looks under the table. She finds the next clue taped to la silla (the chair).
The chair clue says, "Go to la puerta (the door)." Then la ventana (the window). Tomás finds the last clue inside a pencil cup. It is on el lápiz (the pencil).
The treasure is a box of stickers! Rosa holds one up. "¿Qué es? (What is it?)" Tomás smiles. "Es un pájaro (It is a bird)." They named every thing they found.
story.think: Look at the words el libro and la mesa. What do you notice about the last letter?

lessons.title: Book, Table, Chair
lessons.mainIdea: El libro is the book. La mesa is the table. La silla is the chair.
reading: Open your book. It is *el libro* (the book). Put it on the table. The table is *la mesa* (the table).
Now sit down. You sit on *la silla* (the chair). Say it: SI-lla. The ll sounds like y, so say SI-ya.

words.d: the book — you read it
the table — ends in -a, so la
the chair — ll sounds like y: SI-ya

look.title: My Desk
look.text: Look at the classroom. A green book sits on the table. A small chair is next to the table. A red pencil is on the book.
look.prompt: Point to the book, the table and the chair. Say each word in Spanish.

check.why: La mesa means the table.
You sit on a chair. La silla is the chair.
El libro means the book.

lessons.title: The Pencil
lessons.mainIdea: El lápiz is the pencil. It ends in z, not -o.
reading: Pick up your pencil. It is *el lápiz* (the pencil). Say LÁ-pis. The mark on the á makes LÁ loud.
Lápiz ends in z. It does not end in -o or -a. So we just learn it with its partner: el lápiz.

words.d: the pencil — say LÁ-pis

look.title: What Is in My Backpack?
look.cite: Example backpack, made up for practice
look.prompt: How many pencils are in the backpack? Say the number in Spanish.

check.why: El lápiz means the pencil.
We say el lápiz, with a mark on the á.

check.q: Which part of lápiz is loud?
check.why: The mark on á makes LÁ the loud part.

lessons.title: Door and Window
lessons.mainIdea: La puerta is the door. La ventana is the window.
reading: Knock, knock! Open *la puerta* (the door). You walk in and out through the door.
Look outside. You look through *la ventana* (the window). Both words end in -a. Both go with la.

words.d: the door — you walk through it
the window

look.title: A Sunny Room
look.text: The sun shines in the window. The door is open. A cat walks in through the door and naps in the sun.
look.prompt: Point to a door and a window in your room. Say their names in Spanish.

check.why: La ventana means the window.
You knock on a door. La puerta is the door.
Puerta ends in -a and goes with la.

lessons.title: The Bed
lessons.mainIdea: La cama is the bed. You sleep in la cama.
reading: At night you are sleepy. You get into *la cama* (the bed). Cama ends in -a, so it goes with la.
Sing it: la cama, la mesa, la silla. They all end in -a. They all go with la. Hear the pattern?

words.d: the bed — you sleep in it

look.title: Good Night
look.text: It is dark. A girl is in her bed. Her book is on a little table. The window shows the moon.
look.prompt: Say the Spanish word for the bed, the book and the window.

check.why: La cama means the bed.
You sleep in a bed: la cama.
Cama ends in -a and goes with la.

lessons.title: The -O and -A Clue
lessons.mainIdea: Most -o words go with el. Most -a words go with la.
reading: Look at the end of a word. Libro ends in -o: el libro. Mesa ends in -a: la mesa. The last letter is a clue.
It is a clue, not a rule every time. Most -o words go with el. Most -a words go with la. A few words break the clue.

words.d: the — most words that end in -o use el
the — most words that end in -a use la

look.title: Sort the Words
look.text: Two boxes: an el box and a la box. Words to sort: libro, silla, gato, ventana, perro, puerta.
look.prompt: Put each word in the el box or the la box. Use the last letter.

check.why: Most -a words go with la: la ventana.
Libro ends in -o and goes with el.

check.q: What is the clue for el or la?
check.why: The last letter, -o or -a, is the clue.

lessons.title: Two Rule-Breakers
lessons.mainIdea: Día ends in -a but is el día. Mano ends in -o but is la mano.
reading: *El día* (the day) ends in -a. But it goes with el! Buenos días means good morning.
*La mano* (the hand) ends in -o. But it goes with la! Wave your hand. Say la mano. These two break the clue.

words.d: the day — ends in -a but uses el
the hand — ends in -o but uses la

look.title: ¿Qué es?
look.text: Señor Díaz points to a book. "¿Qué es? (What is it?)" Rosa says, "Es un libro (It is a book)." He holds up his hand. Tomás says, "Es una mano (It is a hand)."
look.prompt: Point to a thing in your room. A friend asks ¿Qué es? You answer Es un... or Es una...

check.why: Mano breaks the clue. We say la mano.
Día breaks the clue. We say el día.
¿Qué es? means What is it?

review.why: Mesa ends in -a and goes with la.

review.q: ¿Qué es? Your friend holds a book. You say...
review.why: Libro goes with el and un: Es un libro.
Día ends in -a but uses el.
Mano breaks the -o clue. We say la mano.
